chunks: How smartphone night mode works. The question: How does night mode on smartphone cameras work?
In a dark scene each tiny pixel catches only a few particles of light, so the picture is grainy.
Night mode fixes this by taking a quick burst of short photos, lining them up, and merging them. The merged image has gathered much more light in total, so it is cleaner.
A final step brightens the dark parts.
Suppose you time a sprinter with a stopwatch. One reading is a bit off, because your thumb is a little early or late each time.
Take nine readings and average them, and the error shrinks to a third.
Night mode does the same with light, with one catch: the nine readings must be of the same thing, so the phone first lines up the photos, since your hand moved between them.
Stacking gains about 3 decibels every time N doubles.
The dashed curve is one long exposure with the same total time: it's higher at the lowest light because it pays read noise once, but it cannot be used handheld.
Notice that at higher signal (orange) stacking costs almost nothing compared with a long exposure.
Shot noise: the random ups and downs in how many photons land on a pixel. With few photons, the relative error is large. Burst: several photos taken in quick succession.
Alignment: shifting the photos so the same scene point lands on the same pixel in each. SNR (signal-to-noise ratio): how big the real signal is compared with the random grain.
Tone mapping: brightening the shadows while keeping bright areas from washing out.
Say each short photo collects 25 electrons in one pixel in the dark. Photon noise is about the square root of 25, which is 5, so the signal-to-noise ratio is 5.
Merge 9 aligned photos. Now the pixel has 225 electrons in total, and the noise is the square root of 225, which is 15. The ratio is 15, three times better.
(We ignored the small electronic noise added at each readout.) Why not one long exposure instead? A shaking hand or moving subject would blur it. That is the whole idea.
"Night mode fights photon shot noise by collecting more light than one handheld exposure could.
The phone takes a burst of short frames, picks the exposure length from the gyro so it stays sharp, aligns the frames, and merges them while rejecting moving regions.
Averaging N frames improves SNR by the square root of N. Then it tone-maps to brighten, denoises, and fixes white balance. OIS and fast compute make it practical."
